question: Despite repeated complaints being lodged over the years by individuals, associations and social bodies, the vast majority of Greek sports pitches and stadiums still lack basic infrastructure that would allow spectators with disabilities and other physical conditions/limitations to access these venues independently.

The absence of such infrastructure can be seen throughout any given sports venue, from the surroundings of the sports facilities themselves to the grandstands, which currently have no accessible seating areas. Sports pitches and stadiums are lacking in terms of suitable infrastructure (ramps, lifts, escalators, etc.)

and in terms of staff who can assist those who are unable to look after themselves (people in wheelchairs or with mobility impairments, blind people, etc.) and who need a carer because of their physical condition.

Despite the fact that the complaints made over the the last 30 years, at least, have been accompanied by specific suggestions for improvements, the State has simply responded with empty promises and/or mentions of supposed obstacles, which simply perpetuate the unwillingness to do anything to remedy the situation.
Preventing and excluding people with disabilities from participation in social life is inadmissible and constitutes unacceptable discrimination.

This is made clear in Article 26 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights, Directive 2019/882, the Commission’s Strategy for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2021-2030 and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities adopted in 2006, as well as a host of other binding texts1.
In view of this: What could the Commission do to help ensure that people with disabilities can enjoy full, unimpeded and equal access to sports events in Greece?

For instance, the Commission’s action on accessibility to the built environment, which led to the development of European standard EN 17210, and Mandate 473 on accessibility following ‘Design for all’ standards, which resulted in European standard EN 17161.
answer: The EU Strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities 2021-2030 (2) calls for the implementation of legislation and standards on accessibility, as a prerequisite for the full participation of persons with disabilities in society on an equal basis. It also highlights that accessible and inclusive sport is fundamental.

The European Accessibility Act (3) does not cover the physical accessibility of sport venues as such, but Greece opted in to apply Annex III on the built environment. Also, the EU and its Member States are parties to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and bound to comply with its provisions, including on accessibility (4).

Moreover, the 2019 Council conclusions on Access to sport for persons with disabilities (5) recommend that Member States take action to ensure access of persons with disabilities to sport infrastructure. It included attendance at sport events, training or participation in sport, also through the implementation of accessibility standards.

The 2022 Council conclusions on sustainable and accessible sports infrastructure (6) further encourage Member States to design sports infrastructure that provides barrier-free access to sports for citizens with specific physical accessibility requirements.

For instance, the Commission’s action on accessibility to the built environment, which led to the development of European standard EN 17210, and Mandate 473 on accessibility following ‘Design for all’ standards, which resulted in European standard EN 17161. https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1484&langId=en https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/882/oj (OJ L 151, 7.6.2019). https://social.desa.un.

The Erasmus+ programme promotes the participation in sport of people with disabilities and can fund projects supporting access to sport. European structural and investment funds can also be used to finance the adaptation and improvement of sport infrastructures.
